blocks.text: 7.3 — System Design Mock Interview
Module 7 · Lesson 7.3 — Solution Architect Academy
Learning Objectives

items: Internalize the live system-design interview loop: clarify → NFRs → high-level diagram → deep dive → trade-offs.
Practice thinking out loud and driving the whiteboard.
Produce an end-state architecture with a defensible trade-off discussion.
Use the reusable checklist to self-direct any prompt.

blocks.text: The Live System-Design Interview Format
Unlike a take-home, the live session is you and an interviewer at a whiteboard for 45–60 minutes. There is no single right answer. The interviewer scores your process:

items: Clarify requirements — who, what scale, what's the core use case. Never skip.
Pin down NFRs — latency, availability, consistency, compliance, cost envelope.
High-level diagram — boxes and arrows for the critical path first.
Deep dive — pick the riskiest part (data model, consistency, scaling) and go deep.
Trade-offs — state what you chose and what you gave up, and how you'd evolve it.

blocks.text: Golden rule: narrate your reasoning constantly. Silence reads as "stuck." A "let me think about the read path first" is better than drawing in silence.
Full Worked Mock: "Design an AI Customer-Support Assistant (RAG)"
Below is a realistic transcript. I = Interviewer, C = Candidate (you).
Phase 1 — Clarify (I → C)
I: Design an AI customer-support assistant that answers customer questions using our help-center articles and order data.
C: Great. Before I draw anything, a few questions:

items: Users & scale: ~2M customers, peak ~500 requests/min, mostly web + mobile?
Core job-to-be-done: answer "where's my order" and "how do I return" type questions, citing sources?
Data sources: help-center articles (static-ish) + live order status (dynamic, PII)?
Languages: English only, or multilingual?
Must it take actions (issue refund) or only answer? I'll assume answer-only for v1, with a handoff to a human path.
Latency/availability NFRs: p95 < 3s, 99.9% available?
Compliance: order data is PII — must not leak across tenants.

blocks.text: I: Good scoping. Yes to all your assumptions. 99.9%, p95 < 3s, PII isolation required.
Phase 2 — High-Level Diagram (C narrates while drawing)

C: Here's the critical path. A user asks a question; we retrieve grounding context, generate an answer with an LLM, and return it with citations. Two retrieval paths: a vector store for the knowledge base, and a scrubbed order service for "where's my order." We never send raw PII to the LLM.

blocks.text: I: Why split retrieval into two paths instead of one?

C: Because they have different consistency and privacy needs. The KB is slow-changing, embeddable, and safe to vectorize. Order data is real-time and PII — I retrieve only the authorized customer's order, scrub fields, and pass minimal context. Mixing them in one index would risk leaking PII into embeddings.
Phase 3 — Deep Dive: Data & RAG Pipeline (C drives)
C: Let me go deep on the RAG core, the riskiest part.

items: Tools: LangChain/LlamaIndex, pgvector or Qdrant.
Techniques: hybrid search (keyword + vector) to catch product codes; re-ranking for precision.
Tools: guardrail layer, confidence threshold.
Techniques: tokenization, per-tenant isolation, short-lived session context.
Ingestion: Help-center articles → chunk (≈500 tokens with overlap) → embed → upsert to vector store. Re-index nightly + on publish.
Retrieval: embed the query, similarity search top-K, re-rank, then inject into the prompt with explicit "cite source" instructions.
Grounding guardrail: if retrieval score < threshold, answer "I don't know / hand to human" — this fights hallucination.
PII handling: order context is fetched per-authenticated-user, fields minimized, and never persisted in the prompt store beyond the session.

blocks.text: I: How do you keep answers fresh when articles change?
C: The ingestion job re-embeds on publish and on a nightly sweep; we version the index and can roll back. For hot fixes we support manual re-index of a single doc.
Phase 4 — Deep Dive: Resilience & Scale
I: 500 req/min, p95 < 3s. What breaks first?

C: Two risks: (1) LLM latency/cost — mitigate with a semantic cache (identical questions skip generation), smaller model for easy queries, and async for non-interactive. (2) Vector store load — it's read-heavy and scales horizontally; cache embeddings. The whole RAG service runs behind the API Gateway with Circuit Breaker + Bulkhead so a slow LLM doesn't take down auth or the human-handoff path.
C (cont.): On failure, we degrade: if the LLM is down, return a "search these help articles" fallback with the retrieved links — still useful, no hard error.
Phase 5 — Trade-offs & Evolution (C closes)
C: My key trade-offs:

items: RAG over fine-tuning: fresher, citeable, cheaper to update; cost is retrieval latency + infra.
Answer-only v1: avoids risky autonomous actions; we add a guarded "request refund" later behind human approval.
Single-cloud managed LLM: fastest, but creates dependency — we keep the orchestrator portable so we can swap providers.
Eventual vs. real-time KB: nightly re-index is fine for support articles; real-time only for order status (which is live anyway).

blocks.text: Evolution: add multilingual embeddings, agentic actions with approval, and eval/observability (answer-quality scoring) before scaling further.
I: That's a strong v1. Let's stop there.

blocks.text: Reusable System-Design Interview Checklist
Run this loop on any prompt (booking platform, RAG assistant, payments, IoT ingest):
1. Requirements

items: Who are the users and what is the core use case (1 sentence)?
Read path vs. write path — which dominates?
Clarifying questions asked before drawing.

blocks.text: 2. Capacity & Scale

items: Estimated RPS / storage / growth rate stated.
Peak vs. average distinguished.

blocks.text: 3. NFRs

items: Latency target (p95/p99) stated.
Availability/SLO target stated.
Consistency model (strong vs. eventual) chosen and justified.
Compliance/security constraints (PII, multi-tenant) called out.

blocks.text: 4. Diagram

items: High-level critical-path diagram drawn early.
Components labeled (gateway, services, datastores, async).
Mermaid/whiteboard is readable, not a box explosion.

blocks.text: 5. Data

items: Data model / storage choice justified (SQL vs. NoSQL vs. vector).
Consistency & replication strategy addressed.
Migrations / ingestion considered (esp. AI/RAG or ETL).

blocks.text: 6. Resilience

items: Failure modes identified (what breaks first?).
Patterns applied: Circuit Breaker, Bulkhead, Retry/Timeout, Fallback, Saga where relevant.
Degraded-mode behavior defined (not just "it works").

blocks.text: 7. Cost & Trade-offs

items: Major trade-off stated explicitly (what you gave up).
Cost levers mentioned (cache, commitments, right-sizing, model choice).
Simplicity preferred over trendiness.

blocks.text: 8. Evolution

items: v1 scope vs. future stated.
Clear "how I'd extend" (multilingual, agentic, multi-region).
Observability / eval plan included.

blocks.text: Drill: Pick "Design a scalable ticket/event booking platform." Time-box 45 min: 5 clarify, 10 diagram, 15 deep dive (data + consistency), 10 resilience, 5 trade-offs. Record and critique against the checklist. Then swap with a peer and interview each other.
